extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, history, and constitutional law; general readers of classic political analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of evaluative principles and institutional criteria from a 19th‑century political analysis of American society and government (inheritance law, bail/committal, townships, sovereignty of the people, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committal and bail system disadvantages the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil and criminal procedure of the Americans has only two means of action—committal and bail. The magistrate first exacts security from the defendant, or, in case of refusal, incarcerates him; the ground of the accusation and importance of the charges are then discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This system is hostile to the poor and favorable to the rich: the poor may lack security and be imprisoned while awaiting justice, whereas the wealthy can avoid imprisonment in civil causes and may escape punishment by breaking bail, reducing penalties effectively to fines. (Footnote: 'Crimes no doubt exist for which bail is inadmissible, but they are few in number.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of descent as a primary determinant of social and political institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws governing inheritance (the law of descent) should be placed at the head of political institutions because, although they belong to civil affairs, they exercise an incredible and uniform influence upon the social state and affect generations yet unborn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form of inheritance law (e.g., partible inheritance vs. primogeniture/entail) has major long-term effects: it can concentrate property and power in a few hands (aristocratic tendency) or divide and disperse property and power (democratic tendency). The legislator's regulation of inheritance sets a long-lasting social mechanism in motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partible (equal) inheritance disperses landed property and promotes democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When the law of inheritance decrees equal division of a father's property among children, it tends to perpetually diminish landed property and to destroy the close connection between family identity and estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of effects: a direct physical effect (parcelling and diminution of estates over generations) and an indirect effect on heirs' minds and passions that weakens family pride and the will to preserve estates. Over time, partible inheritance reduces large landed wealth and helps democratize society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entail and primogeniture preserve aristocratic continuity; their removal fosters equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws (like entail and primogeniture) that regulate descent to preserve estates intact unite property and family, perpetuating family names, glory, and power; modifying or abolishing these laws accelerates circulation of wealth and destroys hereditary ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the United States the English laws concerning transmission of property were abolished or modified at the Revolution, enabling free circulation of property and rapid disappearance of hereditary ranks (example: New York retaining only two old families after a generation). See footnotes referencing legal changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic incentives and small proprietors accelerate dispersion of estates
rubrics_metrics.description: Small proprietors often derive more proportional revenue from their land and may succeed in increasing holdings, while large proprietors face pecuniary incentives to sell; thus market calculations tend to prevent re-aggregation of divided estates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where tendencies to accumulate land exist, they are insufficient to recreate great territorial possessions once partible inheritance has fragmented them. Cultural factors and habits in other countries (e.g., France) can slow this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic social condition: equality of fortune, education, and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: American society exhibits marked equality: in fortune, in the level of instruction (primary education widely accessible), and in the professional orientation of life (few can live without a profession; education ends early and is practical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces a 'middle standard' of human knowledge that most approach, resulting in few extremely learned or extremely uneducated people. The social lack of hereditary leisure and sustained intellectual classes means the taste and power for higher intellectual pursuits are uncommon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political consequences of social equality — trend to universal suffrage or to concentrated power
rubrics_metrics.description: Social equality tends to extend equality into the political sphere; there are essentially two political outcomes: (1) every citizen is put in possession of rights (sovereignty of the people), or (2) rights are granted to no one (absolute power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As electoral qualifications are extended, pressures increase to abolish them entirely; each concession strengthens democracy and makes further extension more likely. Democratic impulses can thus lead either to popular sovereignty or, if perverted, to equality in servitude rather than liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty of the people realized in law and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people is recognized by customs and proclaimed by laws; it spreads freely and is developed in many forms (direct lawmaking by the people, representatives chosen by universal suffrage acting almost under immediate control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American society largely governs itself: the nation participates in making and executing laws through choice of legislators and executive agents; administrative power is weak relative to popular origin, and few would seek authority outside the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal (township) institutions are essential to liberty but fragile
rubrics_metrics.description: Town-meetings and municipal independence constitute the strength of free nations; they bring liberty within the people's reach and teach citizens how to use and enjoy it. Municipal freedom is rarely the fruit of design and is easily destroyed by central power or by a highly civilized people skeptical of local independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Township liberties consolidate only after long legal and customary existence; they require support from national manners and public opinion. Without municipal spirit a nation cannot sustain the spirit of liberty, even if external forms of free government exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township size and structure that support effective local government
rubrics_metrics.description: The New England township is described as intermediate between a French commune and canton, with an average population of two to three thousand so that inhabitants' interests do not conflict and capable leaders can be found among citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This population size makes representative systems unnecessary within the township (town-meetings are used instead); exceptions exist for large towns and cities which may have mayors and corporations requiring legal sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local authority arrangement: people as source of power; selectmen and town-meeting governance
rubrics_metrics.description: In New England townships the people are the only source of power; the majority acts by representatives in state affairs, but in townships representation is generally not adopted: there is no corporation and the body of electors directs magistrates in everything beyond ordinary executive business. Most authority is vested in selectmen and exercised via town-meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This local arrangement contrasts with city exceptions (mayor, bicameral corporation) and shows how municipal officers may be obligatory and remunerated. The system depends on direct popular control rather than distant administrative apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical contingency in institutional development — origin and timing matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions like municipal independence and the sovereignty of the people developed from particular historical circumstances (e.g., township customs, colonial origin, the Revolution) and cannot be fully understood without examining those state-level conditions first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore analysis of national/federal institutions should follow study of state and local institutions: the Federal Government is a later modification of pre-existing republican principles of the states, and the township and county are the 'nervous centres' of political life.
